URL: https://www.madgrowth.io/guides/how-to-price-fractional-consulting/
Title: How to price fractional consulting in Europe · Madgrowth

Guide

# How to price fractional and consulting services

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 17 September 2026 · 10 min read

Price fractional and consulting work from two numbers: what the problem costs your client, and what the alternative costs them (usually a full-time hire). Sell a monthly retainer or a fixed-price offer with three options, and keep your day rate as a private floor that no client ever sees.

The short answer
- Fractional and consulting work is priced in three ways: a day rate, a monthly retainer, or a fixed price set from the value of the result. For senior operators I recommend the retainer or the fixed price, because both charge for the outcome and neither counts your hours.
- In the INIMA 2025 European Survey of 800 interim managers, the average billed day rate was 994€, ranging from 534€ in Poland and 612€ in Portugal to 1,302€ in Germany and 1,644€ in Switzerland.
- Dividing your old salary by working days gives a rate that's too low. It assumes you bill every working day and ignores holidays, pension, equipment and the time you spend selling.
- Show every serious prospect three options at once. The top option is there to make the middle one, the one you want most clients to buy, look reasonable.
- Raise prices for new clients when you're turning work down, when prospects accept without pushback, or when you have a new result you can name.

## What are the three ways to price fractional and consulting work?

Fractional and consulting work is priced by the day, by the month, or as a fixed price for a defined result.

A few definitions, so the rest of this guide is precise:

- A fractional executive is a senior leader (a CMO, head of growth, CTO or CPO) who works part-time in an ongoing role for a company, often a few days a month, with the same accountability as an in-house leader.
- A day rate is a fee for each day you work. Clients count the days.
- A retainer is a fixed monthly fee for a defined scope: outcomes, responsibilities, a set number of days, or access to you.
- Value-based pricing sets the fee as a share of what the result is worth to the client. Hours don't enter the calculation. A productized offer applies the same idea to a standard package with a public price.

| Model | Best for | Pros | Cons
| Day rate | Interim roles, workshops, overflow work through agencies | Easy to quote and compare. Buyers understand it straight away. | Caps your income at days times rate. Invites haggling. Clients watch the clock, and getting faster earns you less.
| Monthly retainer | Fractional leadership and ongoing advisory | Predictable income. The client buys a role, which is easier to compare with a hire. | Scope creeps unless it's written down. Weak retainers turn into "call me whenever" at a flat price.
| Fixed price (value-based or productized) | Audits, diagnostics, launches, defined projects | Highest margin when you're efficient. Easy to buy. A productized version can be sold from a page without a call. | You carry the risk if you scope badly. It needs a clear result and a client who can put a number on its value.
Jonathan Stark has made the case against hourly billing for years: it punishes you for getting better. Alan Weiss (Value-Based Fees) and Blair Enns (Pricing Creativity) go further and argue that the fee should follow the value of the result. I agree with both. A day rate is useful as an internal number and a weak thing to sell.

A simple productized example is The Audit on this site: a written diagnosis at a fixed 599€, delivered within 5 business days of confirming the intake. The buyer knows the price, the scope and the date before they pay.

## How much do fractional executives charge in Europe?

Senior interim and fractional leaders in Europe bill roughly 530€ to 1,650€ a day, depending mostly on the country. The INIMA 2025 European Survey (International Network of Interim Manager Associations, 800 interim managers in eleven countries, surveyed in January 2025) reports these net day rates billed on the last assignment, excluding expenses and VAT:

| Country | Average day rate (2024 assignments)
| Switzerland | 1,644€
| Germany | 1,302€
| Austria | 1,210€
| United Kingdom | 1,050€
| France | 1,044€
| Italy | 706€
| Portugal | 612€
| Spain | 590€
| Czech Republic | 546€
| Poland | 534€
| Europe average | 994€
The INIMA 2026 European Survey reports average day rates down 0.9% on the year before, so the table is still a fair guide. In Germany, the DDIM Marktstudie 2026 (Dachgesellschaft Deutsches Interim Management, February 2026) forecasts an average day rate of 1,317€ for 2026.

For fractional CMOs specifically, Primewise's 2026 UK benchmark (interviews with 53 active fractional CMOs, October 2025 to February 2026) puts day rates at £1,000 to £1,300 for CMOs with 10 to 15 years of experience and £1,300 to £1,800 for 15 to 20 years. It puts B2B SaaS and tech at £1,200 to £1,800, and a four-day-a-month retainer at about £60,000 to £80,000 a year.

Three caveats before you copy a number. Most interim assignments are full-time placements, often in industrial companies, while fractional work is part-time, and in my view a part-time senior role can justify a higher effective day rate. INIMA itself notes that an average day rate has limited practical meaning, because there's no average interim. And your rate should follow where your clients are. If you live in Lisbon and sell to scale-ups in Berlin or Munich, the German column is the one to read.

## Why is pricing from your old salary a trap?

Your salary divided by working days produces a rate that's too low, because it assumes you'll bill every working day and it prices your time when the client is buying a result.

Say you earned 110,000€ as a VP. Divided by 220 working days, that's 500€ a day. Here's what that number leaves out:

- Days you won't bill. Selling, admin and gaps between clients take days. Even established interim managers in the INIMA 2025 survey billed 65% of working days on average in 2024. Someone new to fractional work should plan for fewer.
- Costs your employer used to carry. Holidays, sick days, pension contributions, social security as a self-employed person, a laptop, software, an accountant and insurance.
- Risk. A client can end a retainer with a month's notice. Your price has to cover the months between clients.
The bigger problem is the reference point. The client never sees your old salary. They compare your fee with what the problem costs them and with the price of hiring someone full-time. Salary thinking also pulls you into negotiating like an employee asking for a raise. A supplier names a price and explains what it includes.

## How do you work out what to charge?

Work out your price in four steps: set a private floor, put a number on the client's problem, price their alternative, then choose the model that fits how they buy.

### 1. Calculate your floor

Your floor is the revenue you need in a year divided by the days you can realistically bill. Say you need 140,000€ of revenue to cover your pay, pension, tax set-asides, tools and real holidays, and you expect to bill 100 days. Your floor is 1,400€ a day. Below it, you're paying to work for that client. Keep the number out of proposals.

### 2. Put a number on the problem

Ask the client what the problem costs them, in their units: pipeline, revenue, churn, months of delay, a funding round at risk. Weiss argues that you should agree on the value before you mention a fee. If a company needs 500,000€ of new annual revenue and has no one to own growth, a 7,000€ monthly retainer is small next to that number. If the client can't name what the result is worth, your offer needs work first: see what to sell after a career in tech.

### 3. Price the alternative

List what the client would do without you: hire a full-time leader, use an agency, promote someone junior, or wait. A full-time hire comes with recruiting time, a salary, employer costs and often equity, and it takes months before that person is productive. A retainer that costs much less and starts next week is an easy comparison for a founder to make.

### 4. Choose the model

Use a retainer when the client needs someone to own an area over time. Use a fixed price when the job has a clear end, like an audit, a positioning project or a launch. Use a day rate when the buyer insists on it (some procurement teams and interim agencies do) and price it at or above your floor. If you're still deciding between a fractional role and other models, start with how to go fractional or fractional, consulting or software.

## How should you structure three pricing options?

Give each serious prospect three options at the same time, ordered from the most complete to the smallest, and price them so the middle option is the one you want most clients to choose.

This is Blair Enns's approach. It works because of anchoring: people judge a price against the other numbers in front of them, and three prices change the question from yes or no to which one.

- Top option: the full outcome plus more of you: more days, faster response, hands-on work with the team. Price it well above the middle. Some clients will buy it, and its main job is to make the middle look reasonable.
- Middle option: the full outcome. This is the offer you've designed the business around.
- Entry option: the smallest thing that solves the problem that made them call you. It's a real offer with less scope, less access and a longer timeline.
Three rules I'd hold to. Talk through the options on a call before you send anything in writing. When a client asks for a lower price, take scope out and keep the price of each option intact. And stop at three, because a fourth option makes the choice harder.

If you tend to say yes to everything and give extra work away, read the Advisor archetype. That profile's blind spot is undercharging and overdelivering, and three options with fixed scopes fix it directly.

## What does a three-tier fractional offer look like in euros?

Here's an illustrative offer for a former VP of Growth selling to B2B SaaS companies after their Series A, using the 1,400€ floor from above.

| Option | What's included | Price | Effective day rate
| Embedded head of growth | About 7 days a month. Runs the growth team, hires the first marketer, weekly leadership meeting, same-day replies on chat. | 12,000€ a month, 3-month minimum | about 1,715€
| Fractional head of growth | About 4 days a month. Owns the growth plan and targets, weekly check-in with the founder, monthly board-ready report. | 7,000€ a month, 3-month minimum | 1,750€
| Growth diagnostic | About 3 days of work over two weeks. Interviews, data review, written 90-day plan, one readout call. | 5,000€ fixed | about 1,670€
A few things to check in an offer like this:

- Every option clears the floor. The lowest effective rate is still above 1,400€.
- The middle option compares well with the alternative. 7,000€ a month is 84,000€ a year. Say the company's other option is a full-time head of growth costing 150,000€ a year in salary and employer costs, plus a hiring process of several months. The fractional option is the obvious first step.
- The diagnostic can lead into the retainer. A client who buys the entry option has a plan and often wants help carrying it out. You can credit part of the fee against the first month.
- Capacity sets your ceiling. Three clients on the middle option is 21,000€ a month for about 12 billed days, which leaves time to sell and deliver well. Past that point, raise prices or productize.
If you'd like to run these numbers against your own offer, the Pricing skill in The Stack works through the floor, the value conversation and the three options with Claude, using the playbook for services businesses.

## When should you raise your prices?

Raise your prices for new clients as soon as demand for your time is ahead of your capacity. Don't wait for January or for a round anniversary.

The signals worth acting on:

- You're turning work down or starting a waiting list.
- Prospects accept your first proposal without questioning the price.
- You have a new result you can name, with a client willing to be referenced.
- The scope you actually deliver has grown past what the price was set for.
- You've narrowed your positioning. David C. Baker's argument is that specialists earn pricing power.
How to do it without drama:

- Change the price for new clients first. Update your proposals and your page. If new clients keep saying yes at the higher price, you have your answer.
- Move existing clients at renewal. Give written notice well ahead of the renewal date, say 60 days, with the new price and what stays the same.
- Raise in steps you can say out loud. Going from 7,000€ to 8,000€ a month is a normal conversation. Doubling overnight usually means you set the first price badly, so fix the offer and reprice it properly.

## Find the pricing model that fits how you work

The Builder Diagnostic is free and takes about 3 minutes. It shows your Builder Archetype and which business models suit how you like to work, so you know whether a retainer, a fixed-price offer or a product should come first. If you already have an offer and want a written verdict on it, The Audit scores your angle, positioning and offer for 599€.
Take the Builder Diagnostic

## Questions people ask

Should I put my prices on my website as a fractional consultant?

Publish prices for productized offers like an audit or a diagnostic, because a public price lets people buy without a call. For retainers, a "from" figure filters out buyers who can't afford you and leaves room to scope the work properly. Avoid publishing a day rate if you sell retainers, because clients will do the division.

Can I charge German or Swiss rates if I live in Portugal?

Yes, if your clients are in Germany or Switzerland. Clients compare your fee with their local alternatives and with the cost of the problem, and your home address changes neither. In the INIMA 2025 European Survey, average interim day rates were 612€ in Portugal and 1,302€ in Germany, so where you sell matters more than where you live.

How much should I charge my former employer for consulting?

Charge your former employer what you'd charge any other client, set from the problem they need solved. They already know your work, which makes the sale easier and gives you a reason to hold your price. Agree a defined scope and a monthly or fixed fee before you start, so the work doesn't slide back into an unpaid version of your old job.

Should I give my first fractional client a discount?

Avoid a straight discount, because your first price becomes the reference for renewals and referrals. If you need a first client quickly, offer your entry option or a shorter first engagement at its normal price. If you do reduce the fee, show the full price on the invoice with a named, time-limited founding-client discount so the real price stays visible.

How many fractional clients can one person handle at the same time?

It depends on how many days each role needs. At about 4 days a month per client, three clients take roughly 12 days a month, which leaves time for selling, admin and holidays. Work out your billable days first, set a client cap, and raise your price when you reach it.

URL: https://www.madgrowth.io/guides/fractional-consulting-or-software/
Title: Fractional, consulting or SaaS: which to start · Madgrowth

Guide

# Fractional, consulting or software: which business should you start after tech?

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 17 September 2026 · 10 min read

If you need income within a few months, start with fractional or consulting work. Build software when you can go a year or more without it paying you, or when client work already covers your bills while you build.

The short answer
- Fractional and consulting work can pay within weeks, because you sell a skill you've already proven to people who already know you.
- Software usually takes years to reach meaningful revenue: in ChartMogul's 2025 data on 6,525 software companies, 13.4% reached $1M ARR within three years of first charging customers.
- Services income is capped by your calendar. Productized services and software can grow past your hours, in exchange for more upfront work and more risk.
- A sensible sequence for many ex tech leaders is services first, then a productized offer, then software for the buyers you already serve.
- Choose the model whose ordinary week you'd enjoy, because that week is what you'll be doing for years.

## What business models can a tech leader start after a corporate career?

There are six realistic models for someone leaving a senior role in tech: a fractional role, consulting or advisory, a productized service, an agency, software (often micro-SaaS) and an audience or media business. They differ in how fast they pay, what they cost to start and what your week looks like.

Quick definitions, so the rest of this guide is precise:

- A fractional executive is a senior leader who works part-time in an ongoing role for one company, such as head of growth two days a week, usually paid a monthly retainer.
- Consulting or advisory is paid judgment on a defined problem, sold as a fixed-fee project or as a monthly retainer for access to you.
- A productized service is a service sold like a product: the same scope, price, timeline and deliverable for every client.
- An agency is a services business where a team does the delivery and you run sales and the people.
- Micro-SaaS is a small software business, usually self-funded and run by one to three people, selling a subscription to a narrow niche.
- An audience or media business earns from attention: a newsletter, a community, courses or sponsorships.
You can combine them, and I cover combinations further down. First, compare them one at a time.

## How do fractional, consulting and SaaS compare?

Fractional and consulting work are the fastest and cheapest to start, while software and audience businesses are the slowest to pay and the only ones with no hard ceiling on income. The other models sit in between.

The time ranges in this table are my own rough estimates for someone starting with a decent professional network. Treat them as orders of magnitude.

| Model | Time to first revenue | Money you put in | Income ceiling | What you must be good at | Typical week | Best-fit archetype
| Fractional role | Weeks, if people already know what you fix | Close to zero | Days you sell per month × your rate | Senior judgment, fitting into a team fast | Client meetings and Slack across one to three companies | Advisor
| Consulting or advisory | Weeks to two months | Close to zero | Your days, raised by value-based fees | Diagnosing problems, selling engagements, writing clearly | Project bursts with sales calls in between | Advisor
| Productized service | One to three months to design and sell the first one | Low: a sales page and your time | Higher than consulting, because delivery gets faster each time | Packaging, refusing custom work, steady selling | Running one repeatable process and filling the pipeline | Productizer
| Agency | Two to six months, often starting as consulting | Medium: contractors or hires before revenue is steady | Team capacity × margin | Hiring, delivery systems, sales | Managing people, reviewing work, pipeline | Orchestrator
| Software or micro-SaaS | Months to a first payment, years to meaningful revenue | Medium to high: build time, tools, maybe a developer | No hard cap | Product sense, distribution, patience | Building, support, marketing, long quiet stretches | Venture Builder
| Audience or media | Six months or more of publishing before it pays properly | Low cash, a lot of time | No hard cap, tied to reach | Publishing consistently with a clear point of view | Writing, answering readers, running launches | Broadcaster

## How do I choose between a services business and a software company?

Decide on five things in this order: how long you can go without income, how much risk you can carry, how far past your own hours the income needs to grow, which skills you're willing to learn and what you want an ordinary week to look like. The first two usually rule options out. The last three pick between what's left.

### 1. Time to first revenue: how long can you go without income?

Your runway is your savings divided by your monthly costs, and it decides more than preference does. If you're leaving a job with less than a year of runway, start with a model that pays in weeks.

Services pay fastest because you're selling work you've already done in a job, to people who've seen you do it. A former VP of product can sell a pricing review to a founder she knows within a month of deciding to.

Software is slower than it looks. Stripe's 2025 review of Atlas startups put the median time from incorporation to first payment at 34 days. Getting from a first payment to a salary takes much longer. ChartMogul's 2025 SaaS Growth Report (6,525 software companies) found that 3.3% reached $1M in annual recurring revenue within a year of first charging customers, 13.4% within three years and 25.1% within five.

Here's what replacing a salary takes in each model. Say you want 10,000€ a month before tax. Illustrative numbers:

- Fractional: two clients at 5,000€ a month each.
- Productized service: four fixed-price audits at 2,500€ each, every month.
- Micro-SaaS at 49€ a month: 205 paying customers, kept after churn.
Two clients is a few good conversations. Two hundred and five subscribers is a marketing system.

### 2. Capital and risk: what are you putting on the line?

Services risk very little cash, and software risks your time before it risks your money. Each model has its own risk, and it helps to name it before you choose.

- Fractional and consulting: concentration. With two clients, losing one halves your income overnight.
- Agency: payroll. You commit to people before the next retainer renews.
- Software: months of building for demand you haven't confirmed. Hire a developer and it becomes cash too.
- Audience: a year of publishing with no guarantee the readers will buy anything.
If you're still employed, the risk picture changes. Software and publishing fit around a job more easily, because you can do them in the evenings. Consulting and fractional work need you in meetings during business hours, which is hard to hide from a full-time calendar. Whatever you pick, read your employment contract for clauses on outside work and intellectual property before you start, especially for software.

### 3. Leverage: how far past your hours does income need to grow?

Leverage is how much more you can earn without working more hours, and services have the least of it. A fractional or consulting business has a ceiling you can calculate in one line.

Say you charge 1,000€ a day and can bill 12 days a month, because the rest goes on selling and admin. Your ceiling is 12,000€ a month. You raise it in two ways. One is to charge for value instead of time, which is the core of Alan Weiss's and Blair Enns's work on pricing expertise. The other is to narrow what you're expert in, which David C. Baker argues is what lets specialists charge more. My guide on how to price fractional and consulting work goes through both.

Productized services add leverage because delivery gets faster every time you repeat it. Software adds the most, since serving one more customer costs little. Every customer still costs something to acquire, and that cost doesn't shrink on its own.

### 4. Skills: what will you have to get good at?

Every model makes you do one job you probably never did in your corporate role. Pick the one you're most willing to learn.

- Services: selling yourself in a conversation and saying no to work outside your scope. Blair Enns's Win Without Pitching Manifesto is the best short read on this.
- Productized services: packaging. Alex Hormozi's $100M Offers is useful on structuring scope and guarantees so a fixed offer sells.
- Software: distribution and positioning. April Dunford's Obviously Awesome covers positioning, Bob Moesta's work on jobs to be done explains why people switch products, and Madhavan Ramanujam's Monetizing Innovation makes the case for testing price before you build.
- Agency: hiring and writing delivery down so other people can run it.
- Audience: publishing on a schedule, for a long time, with opinions.
Engineering leaders can build the product and still find that the hard part of a small software company is getting it in front of buyers. That job lands on you whether you like it or not.

### 5. Lifestyle: what do you want an ordinary Tuesday to look like?

Picture a normal working day in each model and notice which one you'd look forward to. A fractional Tuesday is back-to-back calls and a team channel that expects replies. A software Tuesday is quiet building, a support ticket and a marketing task you've avoided for a week. An agency Tuesday is mostly other people's questions.

People choose a business model for its best month. You'll spend far more time in its ordinary weeks, so choose the week.

## Is fractional work a real business or a job with more bosses?

Fractional work becomes a business when you have a named offer, more than one client and a repeatable way to find the next client. Without those three, it's a part-time job with less security.

The warning signs are easy to spot. Every engagement starts from a blank proposal. Your rate hasn't changed since you started. All your clients came through one former colleague. The fixes are also clear: write one offer with a fixed shape, cap how many clients you take at once, raise your price when your calendar fills and give yourself a way to be found that doesn't depend on luck. My guide on how to go fractional covers the setup step by step.

## Should I start with services and build software later?

Yes, if you have less than a year of runway: services pay the bills, and client work shows you which problem is worth building software for. The risk is that client work fills every hour and the product never starts.

Rob Walling's stair step approach is the best-known version of this. You start with a simple one-time product sold through one channel, repeat that until it's reliable, then move to recurring software. For ex tech leaders I'd adapt it slightly:

- Services. Sell your judgment to a specific buyer with a specific problem.
- Productized service. Once you've solved the same problem three or four times, fix the scope and publish the price.
- Software. Automate the part of the productized service you repeat most, and sell it to the same buyers.
Three rules make the sequence work. Keep the same buyer across every step, so your network and reputation carry over. Block build time on your calendar before clients can take it, such as one fixed day a week. And set a written trigger for shifting your time, for example when product revenue covers your fixed costs for three months in a row.

Some hybrids are stable on their own and never need to become software:

- A fractional role plus a fixed-price audit that brings in the next fractional client.
- An audience plus a small advisory practice fed by inbound from readers.
- Consulting plus a micro-SaaS tool sold to the same buyers.
My own portfolio mixes both sides: Madgrowth sells advisory and digital products, and Mazo is a software company. Running the two side by side is possible. It needs the calendar discipline above.

## Which business model fits your Builder Archetype?

Your Builder Archetype describes how you like to work, and each of the five archetypes has models that suit it and models that will wear it down. Here's how they match up.

- The Advisor fits fractional leadership, advisory retainers and a fixed-price teardown. Few clients, each paying properly for judgment. The trap is underpricing until you've rebuilt a job.
- The Productizer fits productized services, templates and self-serve courses. Revenue grows with copies sold. The trap is shipping several small things and properly selling none of them.
- The Venture Builder fits micro-SaaS and AI tools in a niche you already know, often funded by consulting at the start. The trap is building for another quarter before talking to a customer.
- The Orchestrator fits a boutique agency or a done-for-you service run by a small team on your playbook. The trap is building delivery for ten clients while the pipeline holds one.
- The Broadcaster fits audience-first businesses: a newsletter, cohort programmes and launches, with advisory work fed by inbound. The trap is growing reach with nothing packaged to sell.
Most people have a primary archetype and a secondary pull. An Advisor with some Venture Builder in them might run fractional work for two years and then build a tool for the problem they kept fixing. That's the stair step from the previous section, chosen to suit how you work.

## Find the model that fits how you work

The free Builder Diagnostic takes about 3 minutes. It tells you your Builder Archetype and which business models suit it, so you can rule out the wrong ones before you spend months on them. If you already have an idea and want a direct written verdict on it, The Audit (599€) covers your angle, positioning, offer and launch plan.
Take the Builder Diagnostic

## Questions people ask

Can I build a micro-SaaS while working as a fractional executive?

Yes, if you protect the build time before clients claim it, for example one fixed day a week that no client can book. Build for the same kind of company you already serve, so your fractional work doubles as customer research. Set a written trigger for when the software gets more of your week.

How much savings do I need before leaving my job to start consulting?

Work it out as runway: savings divided by your monthly costs. Consulting can pay within weeks, so a shorter runway is workable than for software, as long as you have a few people in your network who already know what you fix. If you have no conversations lined up, start the business alongside your job and leave once the first client signs.

Is a productized service better than a monthly retainer?

A productized service grows further past your hours, because the scope is fixed and delivery gets faster each time. A retainer gives steadier monthly income and deeper client relationships. You can also sell both: a fixed-price audit as the way in, and a retainer for clients who want you to carry out the fix.

Do I need a technical co-founder to start a software company after a non-engineering role?

Not always. You can validate demand and price before writing code, and small tools can be built with AI coding assistants or a freelance developer. If the product is the long-term bet, a technical partner reduces the risk that everything depends on outside help.

What is the difference between a fractional executive and a consultant?

A fractional executive holds an ongoing role inside one company, part-time, and owns outcomes like a team or a number. A consultant is hired to diagnose or fix a defined problem, usually for a set project or an advisory retainer. Fractional work looks like a part-time job, and consulting looks like a series of projects.

URL: https://www.madgrowth.io/guides/how-to-build-a-micro-saas/
Title: How to build a micro SaaS from your tech career · Madgrowth

Guide

# How to build a micro SaaS from your tech career

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 17 September 2026 · 10 min read

To build a micro SaaS from a tech career, pick a painful workflow you've run many times at work, sell a fix to the people who still run it before you write much code, and price it for businesses. Expect a first payment within months and several years before it replaces a senior salary.

The short answer
- A micro SaaS is a small, usually self-funded software business, run by one to three people, that sells a subscription to a narrow group of customers.
- The best micro SaaS ideas for tech leaders come from workflows you've owned: the spreadsheet your team lived in, the report you rebuilt every month, the gap between two tools your industry uses.
- Validate a SaaS idea by getting people to pay before the product exists, through pre-sales or a manual "concierge" version you run by hand.
- Price for businesses, in the tens or hundreds of euros a month. In ChartMogul's 2025 retention data, AI-native products under $50 a month kept 23% of revenue, against 70% for those above $250.
- Plan for years: ChartMogul's 2025 growth report found 13.4% of software companies reached $1M ARR within three years of first charging customers.

## What is a micro SaaS, and how is it different from a startup?

A micro SaaS is a software business built to be profitable and small: a tight niche, a small team, no outside investors required, and revenue that can pay its founders well without ever becoming a unicorn. A venture-backed SaaS startup raises money to chase a large market fast, and it needs to become very big for the investment to work.

For someone with a job, that difference matters. A narrow micro SaaS can be built in evenings and weekends. Investors in a venture-scale startup expect full-time founders.

The third option people weigh is a productized service: a fixed-scope service at a fixed price, delivered by you.

|  | Micro SaaS | Venture-backed SaaS | Productized service
| Who funds it | You, then customers | Investors | You, then customers
| Team | 1 to 3 people | Grows with each round | You, maybe a contractor
| Market | One niche you can name in a sentence | A large market with room for a big company | One buyer type with one recurring problem
| Can start alongside a job | Yes | Rarely | Yes, if delivery fits your evenings
| Time to first revenue | Weeks with pre-sales, months without | Months to years | Weeks
| What limits income | Distribution and churn | Capital and execution | Your hours
| What you give up | Speed, and the chance of a huge outcome | Control and much of the equity | Income past your own hours
If you're still deciding, I compare software and client work side by side in a separate guide. This guide assumes you've picked software.

## Where do good micro SaaS ideas come from?

Good micro SaaS ideas come from work you've done yourself, repeatedly, and found painful. Ten years in product, engineering or growth means you know which workflows break, who owns them and what people already pay to patch them. Most technical founders have to guess at that.

Generic lists of b2b saas ideas give you a product and no insight into the buyer. Your work history gives you both. These are the places I'd look.

| Where to look | What it sounds like | Why it works | Watch out for
| The spreadsheet a team runs on | "Ops keeps the renewal tracker in a shared sheet with 40 tabs" | People already do the work manually, so the demand is proven | Some teams like their spreadsheet and won't switch
| The report you rebuilt every month | "Every board pack took two days of exports and copy-paste" | Clear time cost, a clear owner, a clear deadline | A BI tool they already pay for may add it
| The gap between two tools | "Our product analytics never matched what finance saw in billing" | Incumbents rarely build for each other | You depend on two APIs you don't control
| An app store or integration marketplace | "The Shopify or HubSpot app for this is abandoned" | Buyers are already searching inside the platform | Platform fees, and the platform can copy you
| Something you already do for clients | "I run the same pricing audit for every company I advise" | You've been paid for it, so you know it's worth money | Software can't carry the judgment part
| A regulated or compliance-heavy workflow | "Every EU customer asks us for the same data-processing paperwork" | Deadlines and penalties create budget | Errors carry real liability

### Examples by background

These are illustrative patterns, not tested ideas.

- Product leaders: tools that turn scattered customer feedback into a weekly prioritised list for one kind of company, such as B2B marketplaces.
- Engineering leaders: tools for the chores nobody owns, like tracking on-call load across teams or keeping vendor security reviews up to date.
- Growth leaders: reporting that joins ad spend, product signups and billing for a single channel or industry.
If you don't know which part of your career to build from, start with what to sell after a tech job. The same angle can become a service or software.

## How do you validate a SaaS idea before building it?

You validate a SaaS idea by getting buyers to commit money or a firm next step before the product exists. A waitlist signup or an "I'd use that" costs the person nothing, so it proves very little.

### 1. Ask four questions first

- Is there a budget line? Ask what they spent on this problem last year, in tools or contractors. If the answer is nothing, you'll be asking them to find new money.
- Did the problem cost someone something? A lost deal, a missed close, a weekend. That's a painkiller. "It would be nice" is a vitamin.
- Is it a product or a feature? If a tool they already pay for could add it in a quarter, you need a niche that tool won't bother serving.
- Can you reach buyers at this price? Brian Balfour calls this channel-model fit. A 79€ a month product can't pay for a salesperson.

### 2. Interview without pitching

Talk to ten to fifteen people who run the workflow today. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test is the best guide I know: ask what they did the last time the problem came up and what it cost them, and hold back the idea until the end.

### 3. Pre-sell or run a concierge version

A concierge MVP is a version of your product that you deliver manually while the customer pays as if it were software. You run the exports, build the report and send it every Monday. You learn how the work actually gets done, and you find out whether anyone pays.

Pre-sales work the same way: offer a founding-customer deal, such as a discounted annual plan paid now for access when the first version ships. A few people paying in advance tells you more than a hundred signups.

The Stack's Go/No-Go playbook runs this check for software ideas and gives a go, no-go or not-yet verdict with the one assumption to test next. It's part of The Stack, fifteen playbooks that run in Claude.

## Can you build a micro SaaS MVP with AI tools?

Yes. AI coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor and Lovable make it realistic for a product or growth leader to build a working first version, and for an engineering leader to build one in weeks of evenings. The hard part of a micro SaaS is still finding buyers, and AI doesn't do that for you.

- Build only the concierge workflow. The first version should do the one job customers already pay you to do by hand.
- Buy the boring parts. Use an existing service for login, payments and email. Stripe or Paddle for billing, a hosted database, a managed auth provider.
- Take security and privacy seriously early. B2B buyers, especially in Europe, will ask where data is stored and whether you have a data processing agreement. AI-generated code needs a proper review before customer data goes into it.
- Plan for maintenance. Integrations break and dependencies need upgrading long after launch, and that work lands on your evenings too.
AI products can grow quickly. ChartMogul's 2025 SaaS Growth Report found AI-native startups were 3x more likely to reach $1M ARR within 6 months. The same company's retention data, below, shows the catch.

## How should you price a micro SaaS?

Price a B2B micro SaaS against the time or money the workflow costs your customer, usually somewhere from tens to a few hundred euros a month per account, and avoid consumer-style prices like 9€. Low prices attract buyers who churn, and they force you to find far more customers.

The retention numbers are stark. ChartMogul's 2025 SaaS Retention Report, covering 3,500 software companies, found AI-native products priced under $50 a month kept 23% of their revenue over a year (gross revenue retention), while those priced above $250 a month kept 70%.

The maths matters too. Say you want 10,000€ a month in recurring revenue:

- At 19€ a month, you need 527 paying customers.
- At 99€ a month, you need 102.
- At 299€ a month, you need 34.
Thirty-four customers is a list you can build from your network and one niche community. Five hundred needs paid acquisition or a large audience, and you probably don't have either yet.

### How to set the number

- Pick a value metric that grows with the value customers get: per seat, per location, per connected account, per report.
- Talk price during validation. Madhavan Ramanujam's Monetizing Innovation makes the case for testing willingness to pay before you build. Ask what they'd expect to pay, and at what price it becomes too expensive to consider.
- Offer annual plans. Cash upfront pays for the build and gives you a full year to earn the renewal.
- Keep founding prices honest. Discount for early customers, and write down when the discount ends.

## How do you get your first 10 SaaS customers?

Your first 10 SaaS customers usually come from people you already know and from the few places your niche gathers online, through direct conversations you have yourself. Ads, SEO and Product Hunt come later, once you know who buys and why.

- Convert your validation conversations. Everyone you interviewed gets a personal note when the first version is ready, with the founding offer.
- Go through your network by role. List former colleagues who now hold the job that owns this workflow. Ask for a 20-minute call, and ask each one who else has the problem.
- Show up in niche communities. Slack groups, subreddits, LinkedIn groups and associations for your buyers. Answer questions for weeks before you mention the product.
- List it where buyers already search. If you integrate with a platform, the platform's app marketplace is a free, high-intent channel.
- Publish what you learn. Posts about the workflow itself, with numbers from your own experience, bring in the people who have the problem. I cover this in how to build an audience business.
Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" is worth rereading here. Onboard every early customer yourself, on a call, and write down every question they ask.

## How long does it take a micro SaaS to make money?

A micro SaaS can take its first payment within weeks, but reaching salary-level revenue usually takes years. Stripe's 2025 review of Atlas startups put the median time from incorporation to first payment at 34 days. First payments are the easy part.

In ChartMogul's 2025 growth data on 6,525 software companies, 3.3% reached $1M in annual recurring revenue within a year of first charging customers, 13.4% within three years and 25.1% within five. Those that got there usually took between two and five years.

For someone keeping a job, much smaller milestones decide whether it's working. The timings below are my rough estimates, not benchmarks:

- Months 0 to 3: interviews, a concierge version and your first few paying customers.
- Months 3 to 12: a working product, 10 to 30 customers, and enough revenue to cover tools and some of your time.
- Years 1 to 3: a repeatable channel, and the point where you decide whether revenue is high enough to reduce your hours at work.
Rob Walling's "stair step" approach is a sensible way to get there: start with something small that sells through a single channel, then take on a recurring software product once you've learned to sell. Keep your job until the revenue says you can leave.

## Is a micro SaaS the right business for you?

A micro SaaS suits people who want to own a system and can wait for it to pay: in my Builder Archetypes, that's the Venture Builder. If you'd rather have income next month from a skill you've already proven, a fractional role or consulting fits better.

Venture Builders have one predictable blind spot. They keep building for another quarter before talking to a customer, and end up with good architecture and no pipeline. If that sounds like you, put the concierge version and the first ten sales on the calendar before the build.

Some signs it's a good fit:

- You enjoy the product work itself, including the dull parts like support and billing.
- You can give it one steady block of time each week for two years or more.
- You know a niche well enough to name 50 people who'd buy.
- You're comfortable selling directly, at least to the first ten customers.

## Find out if software fits how you work

The free Builder Diagnostic takes about 3 minutes. It shows your Builder Archetype, which business models suit you and which ones will wear you down, so you know whether a micro SaaS is worth your evenings. If it is, The Stack takes you from the go/no-go through pricing and launch.
Take the Builder Diagnostic

## Questions people ask

Can I build a micro SaaS while keeping my full-time job?

Yes, and it's the safer way to start, because the first year rarely pays a salary. Read your employment contract for intellectual property and conflict-of-interest clauses before you build, and keep the work off company laptops and company time. If a clause is unclear, pay a lawyer for an hour before you sign your first customer.

Do I need to know how to code to build a micro SaaS?

Not to start. You can validate the idea and take your first payments with a concierge version you run by hand, and AI coding tools make a simple first version buildable without an engineering background. Once customers depend on it, get an experienced engineer to review security, billing and data handling.

How many customers does a micro SaaS need to replace a salary?

Divide the monthly income you need by your price. Say you want 8,000€ a month before tax and costs: at 49€ a month that's 164 customers, at 149€ it's 54, and at 399€ it's 21. Higher B2B prices make the target reachable through your network and one niche.

Is it better to build a micro SaaS alone or with a co-founder?

Alone works if you can both build and sell, or if AI tools cover the build well enough for your product. A co-founder helps when your skills are one-sided, for example a growth leader who can sell but can't maintain code. Agree on equity, time commitment and what happens if one of you stops before you write anything.

Should I launch my micro SaaS on Product Hunt?

Only after you have paying customers from direct conversations. A Product Hunt launch brings a short burst of attention from a broad tech audience, and the niche B2B buyer a micro SaaS needs is rarely in it. Treat it as a credibility bonus once the product already sells.

URL: https://www.madgrowth.io/guides/how-to-build-an-audience-business/
Title: How to build an audience business and newsletter · Madgrowth

Guide

# How to build an audience business from your expertise

Madalena Rugeroni · Founder of Madgrowth · ex-Google · Updated 17 September 2026 · 10 min read

To build an audience business from your expertise, pick a narrow beat you know from your career, say something specific about it on one platform where your readers already spend time, publish on a schedule you can keep for a year, and move readers onto an email list you control. Design the offer early: at small audience sizes, services and products earn far more than subscriptions or sponsorships.

The short answer
- An audience business earns money from people who follow your work regularly, through sponsorships, paid subscriptions, community, products or services.
- Start with one narrow beat taken from your career and one point of view on it, published on one primary platform at a fixed cadence you can sustain alongside other work.
- Grow an email list you own by turning platform followers into subscribers, with a lead magnet, referrals and cross-promotion with other newsletters.
- Paid subscriptions pay little at small sizes: across beehiiv, the median free-to-paid conversion rate is 0.62% and the median monthly price is $10, so 5,000 subscribers at those medians bring in about $310 a month.
- Services, workshops and digital products are the models that work first for a small expert audience, because one sale is worth hundreds of subscriptions.

## What is an audience business, and is it right for you?

An audience business is a company built on the attention and trust of a defined group of readers, who come back for what you publish and then pay you, or your sponsors, in some form.

For a tech leader with 5 to 10+ years behind them, this usually means a newsletter or media brand about one specific part of the job: B2B pricing, platform engineering, product operations in fintech, growth for developer tools. Anyone can start a newsletter. Very few people have run a pricing change across 4,000 customers, and that experience is what readers come for.

It suits people who like thinking in public and don't mind being visible. In my Builder Archetypes framework that's the Broadcaster: someone whose voice is the distribution and who enjoys the exposure. If you'd rather sell a defined leadership role to two or three companies and never post, going fractional is the closer fit.

An audience grows slowly, so it works best when a job or advisory work pays the bills for the first year.

## How do you pick a beat and a point of view?

Pick the narrowest topic where you have real experience and where a specific group of people has a recurring problem, then take a clear position on how that problem should be solved. A beat is the subject you cover. A point of view is the belief that makes your coverage different from everyone else's on the same subject.

"Leadership" is a category. "Engineering management at Series A to C startups" is a beat. "Engineering managers at that stage should stay hands-on for another year" is a point of view. The beat tells readers whether it's for them. The point of view gives them a reason to pick you.

### Find the beat in your career

List the problems people already ask you about, in Slack, over coffee or on calls you did as a favour. Keep the ones where you've done the work more than once and seen it go wrong. You'll have real stories and numbers to write from, and readers can tell.

Then check each candidate:

- Depth. Can you list 50 issue topics without researching? If you run out at 15, the beat is too narrow or too far from your experience.
- Buyers. Do the readers have budgets, or work at companies that do? Heads of growth at SaaS companies can support sponsors, services and products. Students mostly can't.
- Staying power. Will you still care about this in three years? You'll be writing about it every week.

### Write the point of view in one sentence

April Dunford's positioning work applies to media too: readers judge you against the alternatives they already have. If those are generic newsletters on your topic, your point of view is what they can't get there. Write it as a sentence someone could disagree with.

## Which platform should you start on?

Start on the one platform where your target readers already spend professional time, and repurpose from there to everything else. For most B2B tech audiences that's LinkedIn plus an email newsletter, with podcasts and communities working better as a second step.

The two do different jobs. On LinkedIn, the platform decides who sees each post, which helps you reach new people fast and means your reach can change without warning. On email, you own the list and every issue lands in the inbox, but nobody discovers you there. So publish on LinkedIn to get found, and give people a reason to join your list.

- LinkedIn suits B2B beats read by managers, founders and buyers. I built a LinkedIn audience of over 15,000 followers, and it's where I'd start again for a B2B beat.
- A newsletter on beehiiv, Substack, Kit or similar is the asset you keep. Start it on day one, even with a tiny list.
- A podcast is slower to grow, and good for building relationships with guests who could become clients.
- A community needs an existing audience to seed it, so it's the hardest place to start.
Pick one primary platform and one owned channel. Spreading across five platforms usually costs you the cadence on the one that matters.

## How often should you publish?

Publish at the highest cadence you could keep for 12 months during your busiest quarter, on a fixed day, in a fixed format. For most people with a job or clients, that's one newsletter issue a week and two or three posts a week on the primary platform.

Readers build a habit around a predictable issue, and that habit turns into opens, replies and eventually sales.

What keeps the cadence alive through a bad month:

- A fixed shape. Same day, same structure, similar length. One main idea, one example, one takeaway. Your energy goes into the idea because the format is already decided.
- A buffer. Keep one finished issue in reserve for the week you're sick or travelling.
- A topic bank. Keep a running list of questions readers ask. Replies to your issues are the best source of next month's topics.
- Repurposing. Each issue becomes several posts on your primary platform, each pointing back to the newsletter.
To work this through for your own beat, the Founder Content playbook in The Stack produces your content pillars, point of view, platform choice, cadence and repurposing plan in one document.

## How do you grow a newsletter or audience list?

Newsletters grow through a handful of repeatable methods: converting followers on a social platform, a lead magnet, reader referrals, swaps and recommendations with other newsletters, and appearances in front of someone else's audience. Pick two, do them every week, and track new subscribers by source.

### Turn followers into subscribers

Put the subscribe link everywhere the platform allows it, such as your profile and featured section, and mention the newsletter when a post touches a topic you've covered in depth.

### Offer a lead magnet

A lead magnet is something useful you give away in exchange for an email address, such as a template, a benchmark or a short email course. The best ones are an upgrade to a popular piece: the spreadsheet behind the pricing post, the full question list behind the hiring post. It should also point towards what you'll sell later. The Lead Magnet playbook in The Stack designs one, including the bridge from the free piece to the paid offer.

### Use referrals and cross-promotion

Ask readers to forward the issue, in one line, in every issue. Newsletter platforms have referral programmes and recommendation networks where newsletters suggest each other to new subscribers. Swaps with writers on adjacent beats work well because their readers already read about your topic.

### Show up in other people's channels

Guest posts, podcast interviews, talks and co-hosted webinars put you in front of an audience that already trusts the host. For a tech leader these are often the easiest to get, because hosts want operators with real experience.

## How do you make money with a newsletter?

You make money with a newsletter through five models: sponsorships, paid subscriptions, a paid community, digital products, and services such as advising, workshops or consulting. They start to work at very different audience sizes, and for an expert with a small, specific audience the higher-priced models work first.

Where the table has a number, it comes from beehiiv's public reports. Elsewhere I've left numbers out, because I haven't found reliable public benchmarks.

| Model | How it earns | When it starts to work | Main risk
| Services (advising, consulting, workshops) | A few clients paying high prices | Early, with a small list of readers who hold budgets | Your time caps the income
| Digital products (templates, courses, toolkits) | One-off sales to many readers | Once you know which problem readers ask about most | Building before anyone has asked for it
| Sponsorships | Companies pay to reach your readers, often per thousand opens (CPM) or per click | When you can describe your readers precisely enough that a company wants that exact group | Sponsors your readers don't trust
| Paid subscriptions | Monthly or yearly fees for premium issues or access | At larger list sizes, given a median 0.62% conversion at $10 a month on beehiiv | Churn and the weight of a paid weekly promise
| Paid community | Membership fees for access to peers and to you | After you have an engaged audience to seed it | It depends on you showing up constantly

### What the data says about paid subscriptions

beehiiv's State of Paid Newsletters 2026 report, based on first-party data from thousands of publications, puts the median free-to-paid conversion rate at 0.62%, the median monthly price at $10 and the median yearly price at $100. The top 10% of technology newsletters convert 5.55%. The typical creator launched a paid tier 45 days after starting, and subscriber count doesn't meaningfully change the price.

At those medians, the maths looks like this:

| Subscribers | Paying at 0.62% | Monthly revenue at $10
| 1,000 | 6 | about $62
| 5,000 | 31 | about $310
| 20,000 | 124 | about $1,240
Compare an illustrative services offer. Say 2,000 people read your newsletter on B2B pricing and you sell a 3,000€ pricing workshop to their companies. Two bookings a quarter is 24,000€ a year. At the medians above, 5,000 subscribers pay about $3,700 a year. So I'd put a service or product first and add subscriptions or sponsors once the list is big enough for them to matter.

The first dollar comes faster than people expect. beehiiv's State of Newsletters 2026 report says the median newsletter launched on the platform in 2025 earned its first dollar in 66 days. A living income takes longer, and it depends on the offer.

## Why do audiences without an offer stall?

An audience without an offer stalls because readers have no next step, you can't tell whether the work pays off, and motivation fades after a year of unpaid weekly publishing. If you're good at content, it's the trap to watch for most.

It tends to go like this. Followers go up, people leave kind comments, and selling starts to feel like it might spoil the goodwill. The offer gets pushed to "when the audience is bigger". A year later there are 8,000 followers, no revenue and no idea what anyone would pay for.

- Decide the first offer before issue one. It can change later. Knowing it shapes what you write and who you write for. If you don't know what to sell yet, read what to sell after a career in tech.
- Mention it from the start. A one-line footer ("I run pricing workshops for Series A SaaS teams, reply if that's you") teaches readers that you sell something.
- Treat replies as research. When readers ask for help with the same problem more than once, you've found a product. Bob Moesta's jobs-to-be-done interviews help you find out what made them ask.
If your offer is a template, course or toolkit, the guide on how to sell digital products covers packaging and pricing.

## How do you start a media company alongside a job?

Start a media company alongside a job by running it as a weekly publishing habit for the first six months, with one beat, one platform, one newsletter and one offer, and add people or formats only once readers and revenue justify it. Before you publish, check your employment contract for rules on outside work.

- Weeks 1 to 2. Choose the beat, write the point of view sentence and list 50 topics. Write the first offer in one paragraph. Set up the newsletter and a simple subscribe page.
- Weeks 3 to 4. Write three issues before announcing anything, so you start with a buffer. Build one lead magnet from your strongest topic.
- Weeks 5 to 12. Publish one issue a week and two or three posts a week. Ask for forwards in every issue. Line up one guest appearance or newsletter swap a month.
- End of week 12. Review subscribers by source, the issues with the most replies and the questions people asked. Pitch the first offer to the readers who replied most.
By then you'll know whether you enjoy the weekly rhythm and whether readers respond to the beat, which tells you more at this stage than the subscriber count.

## Find out if an audience business fits how you work

The free Builder Diagnostic takes about three minutes and shows your Builder Archetype, including whether you're a Broadcaster, and which business models suit you. If it points to media, the Founder Content and Lead Magnet playbooks in The Stack help you plan your beat, cadence and first offer.
Take the Builder Diagnostic

## Questions people ask

How many subscribers do you need to make money from a newsletter?

There's no fixed number, because it depends on what you sell. At beehiiv's median paid conversion rate of 0.62% and a $10 monthly price, subscriptions need thousands of readers to add up to much. A service or workshop sold to readers who hold budgets can pay from a much smaller list, because one sale is worth hundreds of subscriptions.

Should I start my newsletter on Substack, beehiiv or LinkedIn?

Pick the social platform where your readers already are for discovery, and an email platform such as beehiiv, Substack or Kit for the list you own. For a B2B tech beat that's usually LinkedIn plus one email tool. Compare the tools on subscriber export, referral features and paid options, then commit to one and keep publishing.

Can I write a newsletter about my industry while I'm still employed?

Usually yes, if your contract allows outside work and you keep your employer's confidential information out of it. Read the clauses on outside activities, public statements and intellectual property first. Write from patterns across your career, and don't name your employer or its clients without permission.

How long does it take to grow a newsletter audience?

Longer than most people expect, so plan for at least a year of weekly publishing alongside other income. beehiiv reports that the median newsletter launched on its platform in 2025 earned its first dollar in 66 days, and a full income takes much longer. After 90 days, judge progress by replies, forwards and where subscribers come from, as well as the total.

Should a new newsletter be free or paid?

Start free unless your beat is one where readers already pay for information, because a free list grows faster and gives you people to sell to. beehiiv's 2026 data shows the typical creator launched a paid tier 45 days after starting. For an expert, a free newsletter with a clear service or product offer gives you more ways to earn early on than a paywall.
